note_tweet.text:
crypto made it possible to launch almost any asset onchain, but most markets still work exactly the same way. create a token, pair it with liquidity, collect fees and hope trading activity follows.

programmable markets open up a much bigger design space.

imagine a memecoin that automatically accumulates BTC or tokenized NVDA from trading fees. that treasury could deploy capital into DeFi, earn yield, provide liquidity or fund buybacks, all according to predefined rules.

now add agents that can monitor liquidity, manage treasury allocations and execute strategies within limits enforced by smart contracts.

suddenly a token can have its own balance sheet, revenue streams and autonomous operations without needing someone manually managing everything.

and this gets more interesting as tokenized stocks, perps, yield-bearing assets and other onchain positions become available as building blocks.

the next wave of DeFi could be less about launching new assets and more about inventing entirely new ways for markets to behave.

We are now going to witness the consequences of David Miller's so-called 'victory' in his employment tribunal that resulted in a ruling that his anti-Zionist views constituted a legally protected philosophical belief under the equality act 2010.

There is a moderate likelihood of some success in the below reported case of *some* Jewish Green Party members plans to sue the Green Party. 

On the merits there are three possible foundations and there is a higher likelihood of an EHRC finding of unlawful acts, but this is not guaranteed, especially if the challenge is purely on the policy text itself, and also because there are only a very small number of claimants.

There is a possibility that a court could rule the Zionism is Racism motion to be a discrimination related to belief. 

Zionism, if argued in a court as defined by the claimants under the broad sense of supporting Jewish self-determination and a Jewish nation-state in their historic homeland, is highly likely to qualify as a protected philosophical belief if it meets the Grainger criteria.

As such, the court could determine that treating Zionism as inherently racist and subjecting holders of a belief in Zionism to detriment because of that belief could amount to direct discrimination. 

This is where the David Miller case quite literally hamstrings the Green Party motion and any other attempt to declare Zionism as racism; Anti-Zionism has already been held to be a protected belief (Miller v University of Bristol), confirmed by the Employment Appeal Tribunal. 

Given anti-Zionism is held to be a protected philosophical belief it follows that Zionism can also be protected precisely because the issue is unlawful treatment of holders of either belief. 

Another possibility is that a court could rule indirect racial and/or religious discrimination. 

Presently, a majority of British Jews identify as Zionist (JPR tracking data showed this to be around 66% in 2025). The policy as adopted, especially after the rejection of a safeguarding amendment that would have protected members affiliated with Zionist-leaning synagogues or Jewish institutions, could be argued to disproportionately disadvantage Jewish members by creating risk of discipline, exclusion, or a hostile environment linked to what can easily be described as an ordinary communal practice (attending synagogue or community events).

The third possible merit on which a court could rule is that of harassment of Jews. 

If a pro-Israel/Zionist Jew can successfully argue that there is an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating, or offensive environment related to race or belief as a result of the Green Party policy then this might result in a ruling of harassment. 

The allegations of an intimidatory conference atmosphere, aggressive chants, and the policy’s framing have been cited in complaints made to the police and the EHRC - even if those complaints have come from politicians in Labour and the Lib Dems (I hope we can begin to see how the stage is being set here). 

In effect, the motion as passed at Green Conference could potentially contravene the Equality Act. A case brought by a Jewish member of the Green Party would have a decent chance of success because a court could decide that there is both belief discrimination against Zionists and indirect racial discrimination against Jews more generally as a result of this motion. 

To summarise, the combination of the Equality Act’s application to parties, the precedent set with the EHRC in the Labour Party case, and expert legal opinion from practitioners who know this area, are all saying that the combination of (1) majority Jewish identification with Zionism, and (2) the rejected safeguarding amendment makes a credible case.

All of the above is not a certainty, however - especially if the evidence presented remains limited to policy adoption rather than proven hostility, intimidation, or harassment.

1/2
